articles.title: Democratic Senator Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke, chief of staff says
articles.summary: U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff said in a statement on Sunday. The 53-year-old Democrat was taken to a hospital on Saturday after he started to feel numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game, said Allison Herwitt, Murphy's chief of staff. ABC News - PHOTO: Sen. Chris Murphy, pictured here in this appearance on ABC's "This Week," Feb. 9, 2025, was hospitalized, Oct. 31, 2026, after suffering a stroke, a top aide to the Connecticut Democrat said. Upon examining Murphy, doctors determined he had suffered a stroke, Herwitt said, adding that the senator has been transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. "The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said. No further information was released about Murphy's condition. For the past several weeks, Murphy has been traveling the country campaigning for Democratic candidates in Tuesday's midterm elections. He was scheduled to appear Sunday with Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, according to the New Hampshire Democratic Party. Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says In 2024, Murphy won his third term to serve Connecticut in the U.S. Senate and has been viewed by some Democratic party officials as a possible candidate for president in 2028. Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont released a statement on social media on Sunday saying he and his wife, Annie, are keeping Murphy and is family "in our prayers." "Just two days ago, I was with Senator Chris Murphy doing what he loves most: Encouraging Connecticut residents to make their voices heard and vote on Tuesday," Lamont said. "There is no stronger advocate for our democracy. And no one who fights harder for the people of this state. Chris is a great friend to Connecticut and to me personally." "I am sure that he will be walking across the state again very soon. And we will all be cheering him on," Lamont added. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates. articles.title: All 9 people on board plane killed after it crashes in Florida, federal officials say
articles.summary: Federal authorities said that the plane crash Sunday near Greenacres was a Learjet with nine people aboard and had departed Austin, Texas and was headed to the Bahamas. The plane crashed into a mobile home neighborhood around 12:50 p.m. in the area of Military Trail and 10th Avenue North, causing major destruction, including fires and scattered debris. All nine people aboard the plane died, Sean Duffy, the U.S. secretary of transportation, said in a post on X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, made just before 4 p.m. He called the crash a "horrific tragedy." More: 'We're gonna crash! ... 'We're out of time' among last words from pilot More: Thunderstorms were firing on Sunday near where a Lear jet went down The FAA said the Learjet 60 departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. “We’re out of time,” the pilot can be heard saying in air traffic control audio circulated online shortly before the Learjet crashed near Greenacres. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate. The NTSB will be in charge of the investigation and will provide all updates. The incident closed all lanes of Military Trail in the area of Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said. FL | PALM BEACH COUNTY First VIDEO of unknown type plane crash in Greenacre. @EmergencyStream pic.twitter.com/M2fsW45I9h — EmergencyStream (@EmergencyStream) November 1, 2026 Authorities said motorists should are avoid the area and seek alternate routes. Postings on Facebook show a fairly wide swath of area spotted with fires, debris and what looks like a crater in the ground. A video circulating online of a plane making a nosedive into the ground is said to be the Learjet, but The Palm Beach Post is not sharing that video as it has not been confirmed. The video is said to be from a driver's dashcam video. The cause of the crash is unknown. Some chatter on social media raised the suspicion that the plane could have been shot down because flight restrictions were in place as President Donald Trump was in town this weekend . Trump departed President Donald J. Trump International Airport for Iowa around noon. More Aftermath of Palm Beach County plane crash. @EmergencyStream pic.twitter.com/kxN1AzltLa — EmergencyStream (@EmergencyStream) November 1, 2026 The Palm Beach Post reported recently that military air defense systems have been positioned around the president's Mar-a-Lago club and home and the surrounding area. Planes that fly into the restricted airspace are diverted, usually by military jets. Multiple planes have violated the airspace since Trump first took office, but a plane has never been shot down in Palm Beach County because of the airspace violations. The upgraded security systems, a pair of Avenger Air Defense Systems , are positioned on a floating barge in the Lake Worth Lagoon on the west side of the seawall next to Trump's Mar-a-Lago. A separate bank of Avenger Air Defense Systems are positioned on the south side of Trump international airport, near the area where Air Force One parks during Trump's visits to Palm Beach. Aircraft Incident. Military Trail between Cresthaven and 10th Avenue N closed to all traffic. Avoid the area. This will be an extended incident. pic.twitter.com/lhl6yY1A0U — PBC Fire Rescue (@PBCFR) November 1, 2026 Each Avenger comprises a modified Humvee equipped with a rotating turret that has two pods capable of launching short-range infrared-homing Stinger missiles, according to a U.S. Army website. The Avenger's targets could include cruise missiles, drones, helicopters and low-flying and high-speed fixed-wing aircraft, according to the Army. As of Sunday night, there was no indication the Learjet was shot down. Weather conditions in the West Palm Beach area on Sunday afternoon were rough with thunderstorms widespread because a stalled frontal boundary parked over the area, pushing freezing cloud tops tens of thousands of feet high — a situation that can cause icing trouble with equipment but also from severe turbulence. The crash site is in an unincorporated area near Greenacres and Palm Springs. The Village of Palm Springs said it has officials on the scene monitoring any effect the crash will have on water and sewer services. If residents experience disruptions, they should call the Utilities Department at (561) 584-8200. Check back for updates on this Breaking News story. articles.title: Judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit seeking to block Alaska Senate certification if GOP loses
articles.summary: A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, two days before Election Day. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote that the relief the government sought was “infeasible” because many ballots have already been cast and mixed together, the AP reported . She also wrote that the government “provides no workable plan” for separating ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan and investigating them “in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy.” Gleason found the federal government did not have the ability to bring the case, NPR reported . Justice Department attorneys are expected to appeal, according to NPR. The ruling does not end the criminal investigation into how the second Sullivan got on the ballot. It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska. One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .) But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department sued last month in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes. Then, on Oct. 28, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." "The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." Matthew Salisbury, a former congressional candidate and Alaska insurance manager, told the Times that he was approached by a man claiming to represent wealthy donors who wanted him to run for Senate as an independent candidate. Salisbury said he met with the man over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, but ultimately declined after being unable to verify his identity. "I'm not naïve," he said. In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social . Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering an investigation to determine whether the alleged effort violated state law. "Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy said in a statement . "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections." Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican who has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2002, wrote in a statement that the people of her state deserve a full explanation. "Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments," she wrote. "By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong." Sam Curtis, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, told CNN that the revelations in the Times report did not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. "Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," Curtis said, adding that the report has "no impact on the current litigation." Rep. James Comer, the Republican head of the House Oversight Committee, said Oct. 29 that the committee is "taking action" to launch an investigation into the matter, including an inquiry into whether any crimes may have been committed. ABC News also reported Oct. 29 that the DOJ had issued a wave of new subpoenas as it probes whether the alleged recruitment scheme may have run afoul of federal conspiracy laws. On Friday, Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for Alaska, confirmed there is a criminal investigation, saying it had been underway for months. He said the Times report led to a "significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, but declined to say what crimes are being examined and said he was "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed," according to CBS News . Before the ruling, the Justice Department had also asked Gleason to order state officials to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan" so it could investigate possible voter confusion, and it requested action before Monday . State attorneys had asked the judge to dismiss the case, arguing that the ballot already distinguishes the two men. It lists the senator as Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican and the incumbent, and the challenger as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party, the AP reported . In a filing Saturday, Alaska's Republican-run government urged Gleason to dismiss the case, calling it a "meritless lawsuit" and the ballot request "both disturbing and impossible" because it couldn't be carried out without violating voter privacy, the AP reported . "Not every wrong can be righted in federal court," the state wrote. The Trump administration says it is trying to combat fraud. On Friday, a federal appeals court rejected a similar DOJ request in California to set aside disputed ballots. An FBI agent also visited the Petersburg business of a Sullivan donor to ask whether he had been misled, the AP reported . The donor said he hadn't. "Everybody knows who the incumbent is," he said. At a rally in Daytona Beach, Fla., on Friday, Trump said Peltola "should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted," adding that Attorney General Todd Blanche would make his own decision, MS NOW reported . No one has been charged. Peltola said at a rally in Anchorage that she was "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." Asked whether someone on her campaign could have been involved, she told KTUU, "I honestly have no idea." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement, and Dan J. Sullivan has long denied running at Democrats' behest. On CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, Sen. Sullivan said he doubted Peltola’s denials. “There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” he said. Asked about certification, he said, “I’m going to accept the results of the election.” Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who leads the GOP’s Senate campaign arm, said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that criminal charges might make sense. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent of Vermont, said on CBS’ “Face the Nation” that what Democrats did “seems to me to be pretty dumb,” adding, “It’s not illegal.” Dunleavy, the Republican governor, suggested his state investigation could still affect the outcome. “If we find out there’s wrongdoing, and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that’s what happens,” he told NewsNation on Friday. The outcome of the fight could still have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a move to block or erase a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency. How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story. How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal." But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report . How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ). For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name. How the Senate candidates will appear on Alaska's midterm ballot. elections.alaska.gov The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two." But according to the Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages. For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication. The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort. The Trump administration's lawsuit Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last month. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said last month of the lawsuit. The suit argued that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead. Democrats asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, also moved to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Oct. 26, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day. Before Gleason's ruling, many legal experts said the lawsuit had a slim chance of success. First, it required a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts said, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters did not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected. "I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon . Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures. "The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said. More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections. "This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media . What's next? Voters decide the race Tuesday. The Justice Department is expected to appeal Gleason’s ruling, while the federal criminal investigation, Dunleavy’s state investigation and the House Oversight Committee’s inquiry continue. An appeal would likely only matter in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans. Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat." articles.title: At 11th hour, Dem Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Mich. Senate race
articles.summary: DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary , Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. “Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.” El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he's focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living. “At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding later: “None of this matters." Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year's most important races. Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker . El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term. Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds. Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded. Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.” Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support. Their appearance came days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party's nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters. “We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement. The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.” “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Hertel wrote, and won't let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Hertel later wrote that Stevens "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers. “This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post. Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’ Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began. Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that. “I'm the one who pulled it, because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in an interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.” In the August primary, Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition. Early voting for Tuesday's election has been underway since Oct. 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan. How did we get here? The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women. Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his primary win. Last week Stevens’ fiance told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.” But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.” El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.” He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.” Trump and Republicans revel in the discord Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.” “Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!” Appearing with Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers. Johnson said he “encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth.” A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers. ___ Cappelletti reported from Washington. articles.title: 2 days before the election, poll shows voters overwhelmingly want change
articles.summary: NBC News Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month ’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture. When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain. But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%. After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). “The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies. Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war. Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year. Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security. “Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now. Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years. Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election. Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections. That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks. It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular. Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties. Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year. “Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response. “I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added. Republican disappointment Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year. Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%. Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises. Trump still maintains an important hold on his base, with near-unanimous job approval (93%) among Republicans who say they support the MAGA movement. But he’s slipped significantly with Republicans who don’t consider themselves part of the MAGA movement: 54% of them approve and 46% disapprove of his performance. Meanwhile, 20% of those non-MAGA Republicans say they prefer to see Democrats control Congress after this election. The president has seen other important voting blocs drift away, too. His net approval rating has dropped 18 points among white voters without college degrees compared to the first NBC News poll of his second term , in 2025. He’s also seen significant declines among young voters and Latino voters, groups that he overperformed with on his way back to the White House in 2024. One of Republicans’ big advantages in 2026 is a favorable political map: Democrats have to win back districts and states Trump won in 2024 to take back Congress. In the Senate, they need to win at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins. But the president’s approval rating is underwater in states he won in 2024: 53% of registered voters there disapprove of his job performance, while 47% approve. In March 2025, his approval rating in those states was 10 points higher. Democratic warning signs There are some warning signs for Democrats, on top of the fact that a lower share of voters have positive views of the Democratic Party compared to the Republican Party. The fight for control of the House and especially the Senate will take place in Trump-won areas, and Republicans are leading on the congressional ballot in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024. The big question is whether that’s enough to withstand shifts in some key places. Government corruption has been a central theme of Democrats’ message this year, but voters narrowly trust Republicans to better handle the issue by 5 points. Even so, Democrats are leading on the congressional ballot among the 28% of voters who do not trust either party on the issue. Republican leaders in Congress are also slightly better off than their Democratic counterparts, but that’s mostly because voters don’t know how to feel about them. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has the highest positive rating of congressional leaders: 24% have positive views of him and 34% have negative views. Just 10% of voters have positive views of Johnson’s counterpart across the Capitol, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, while 22% view him negatively. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is viewed positively by 18% of voters and negatively by 35%. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who’s led Democrats in the body for almost a decade, is far better defined — to his detriment. Just 13% of voters view him positively, and 53% view him negatively. “It’s not great for the Democrats … for 2028,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, when asked about the low marks for Democrats. “But I don’t see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers.” Half of voters have negative views of tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has emerged as one of the most prolific Republican donors in the country over the last two years, while 34% view him positively. Voters are more split about a pair of prominent progressives, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Sanders is more popular: 41% view him positively and 42% view him negatively, while Ocasio-Cortez’s numbers stand at 31%-42%. Democrats hold a significant lead in the battle for Congress despite those factors. But there are indications throughout the poll that the party’s lead is propped up strongly by anti-Republican sentiment, not warm feelings for Democrats. Voters who want Democratic control of Congress are divided between whether their vote is more in favor of Democrats or driven more by opposition to Republicans. “Get your s--- together, Democrats,” an Ohio Democratic woman said when asked what message she wanted to send with her vote this year. “I’m voting for you, but work it out.” The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Oct. 28-30 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. articles.title: Pete Hegseth is facing a new threat — and it's not just from Democrats
articles.summary: Earlier this year, Senate Republicans decided to tighten the screws on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The Pentagon had, for months, stonewalled lawmakers' request for materials related to the military's deadly targeting of alleged drug traffickers in Latin America. So this spring, the GOP-led Senate Armed Services Committee made a threat: grant access to the documents or it would block one of the Trump administration's political nominees. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Hegseth relented, said two people familiar with the exchange, speaking like some others on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations and the secretary's standing with Congress. Spokespeople for the committee and the Pentagon declined to address questions about the episode. The standoff, which has not been previously reported, illustrates Hegseth's increasing susceptibility to congressional oversight and how he might attempt to navigate a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill should Democrats prevail in this week's midterm elections. With limited exception, Republican lawmakers have declined to stand in Hegseth's way while he has purged dozens of senior military leaders he's deemed disloyal, waged an eight-month war in Iran without the consent of Congress and pursued an unprecedented campaign against the illicit drug trade. Democrats would give Hegseth far less room for maneuver once the next Congress convenes in January. Already, some are threatening to investigate and try to remove him from office if they reclaim a majority. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement that, "despite threats of sham witch hunts," Hegseth is "100% committed" to leading the Defense Department "until the end" of President Donald Trump's term and to advancing the president's agenda for the military. The secretary "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," Parnell said, adding that the department under Hegseth "has followed the law." Rep. Adam Smith (Washington), the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said in an interview that, as chairman, he would probe three areas: military operations, politicization of the armed forces and potential corruption in the Pentagon's awarding of defense contracts. The Defense Department is readying for such inquires. Those preparations include accounting for the likelihood that if Democrats take charge they will summon military officers to testify on Capitol Hill, people familiar with the matter said. Hegseth faces a more imminent challenge, though. When lawmakers return to Washington later this month, the House will probably vote on an effort to impeach him over the Iran war. That effort is being led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie (Kentucky), a frequent critic of the administration. "There's a decent chance that it could pass the House, and I think that would be a stain on his record," Massie said in an interview. "If he's contemplating leaving, this would be a good time to do it." The House vote is expected to be close, but the effort is highly unlikely to result in a conviction if it advances to the Senate for a trial. Some officials in the administration and in Congress have mused recently that Hegseth may leave the Pentagon if Republicans lose heavily in the midterms - either to avoid congressional scrutiny or to pursue potential political ambitions. It's possible, too, that the president could remove Hegseth if voters punish the GOP over the Iran war, though Trump has said he stands by him. Two people familiar with Hegseth's thinking said the secretary wants to stay in office for four years. One said it's "silly" to think Democrats having greater control on Capitol Hill will change that. The other person said that Hegseth's September address to hundreds of service members in Quantico, Virginia, was meant to be a road map for his next two years in office, including priorities such as building a new U.S. military base and adopting advanced weaponry. An impeachment would be difficult for Hegseth if he does not stay in office, with significant legal costs and less control over what the Defense Department provides to congressional investigators, another person said. Asked by a reporter Thursday about the prospect of an impeachment, Trump - twice impeached himself - called the threat against Hegseth "terrible" and repeated his confidence in the secretary. "He's a great warrior," the president said. Some Democrats acknowledged being concerned that, should they regain a majority in Congress, repeatedly targeting Hegseth could imperil their ability to compromise with Republicans on critical defense legislation. Still, many of those who sit on the committees that oversee the Pentagon say that Hegseth hasn't worked with them for his two years in office. "Since I became ranking member, I have had the cellphone number of every single secretary of defense," said Smith, who has held the prominent House role for nearly 16 years. "Hegseth does not speak to me." Others in the party have vowed to oust Hegseth. Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colorado), told reporters in October that he would do "everything possible" to remove Hegseth if Democrats retake the House. Hegseth's defenders say they loathe the thought of Trump giving the Democrats "a scalp" by forcing him out, one administration official said. With the president's support, Hegseth has survived multiple controversies, including his use of the commercial messaging app Signal to share highly sensitive details on an imminent military strike and the military's decision to kill two people who survived a strike on an alleged drug boat. But in recent weeks, members of both parties have grown more willing to confront Hegseth, signaling they will block his preferred choices to lead the Army and denouncing his call to live-stream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who committed a mass killing at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. Current and former officials familiar with the Pentagon's standing on Capitol Hill said that Hegseth's challenge after the midterms will be to shore up bipartisan support for the military and defend his record as lawmakers from both parties have grown more critical of him. Two of the officials asserted that Hegseth could work across party lines, depending on how aggressive Democrats were in their investigations. Still, several others predicted that his critics, both in Congress and in the Pentagon, could feel more emboldened to oppose him if Democrats take power. "Pete has made so many enemies - and uncontrollable enemies," one person familiar said. articles.title: Shootings across 5 states leave 6 dead and at least 36 injured over Halloween weekend
articles.summary: Mass shootings over the Halloween weekend — largely in nightlife districts across the U.S. — left at least six people dead and dozens injured, officials said. The deadliest violence occurred in Dallas, where a handful of shootings in the city's Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music and restaurants, killed four people and injured 15 others, police said. Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts. Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators were still trying to determine if three separate shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related, and it wasn't immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved. “This is a really big scene. It's spread out,” Comeaux said. The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured. One shooting happened after a football game in Alabama In Birmingham, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual “Magic City Classic” football game on Saturday night, Mayor Randall Woodfin said at a news conference Sunday. Two were listed in critical condition Sunday, fire officials said. Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division. Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue. The circumstances of the shootings were unclear, and it was also unclear where the fatality occurred. Police spokesperson De'Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and that “multiple weapons” were found. Shootings in other nightlife districts In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said. Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city’s Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment and their conditions were not available. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available. A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries of an unknown nature that were not life-threatening. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. In Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting early Sunday near the University of Arkansas. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting. Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan. Police said a shooting inside a store in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. There were no immediate arrests. In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon. A man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said. ___ Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report. articles.title: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but the stock market's sweetest stretch might be now
articles.summary: The AI trade just had its scariest October in years. The rest of the stock market barely noticed. The biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) have each given up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel ( INTC ) lost nearly half its value in October. Everything else? The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion. And while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped this week, 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that hadn’t happened in any week since at least 1999, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Yahoo Finance Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac , has a name for this: "Octoberphobia." And he's buying the sell-off. "I did buy some today... this is an opportunity here," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Friday . "The damage isn't as bad as the headlines are." Hirsch also has the calendar on his side. October selloffs like this one often lead into what the Almanac calls the sweet spot of the presidential election cycle , which runs from the fourth quarter of a midterm year through the following June. History is on the buyers' side From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950 , with a median gain of about 15%. Chip stocks have been 8-for-8 since 1994, with a median gain of about 22%. Yahoo Finance The ride wasn't always smooth. Chips fell another 11% or so before turning higher in 2002 and 2018, and eight cycles is a relatively small sample. Chips just sprang a possible bear trap The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) tumbled about 17% in October, yet it's still up more than 50% this year. On Friday, it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom. Then it closed at $472, back above that line. That's the look of a bear trap — a breakdown that reverses, catching traders betting on more losses. Chip stocks briefly broke below their July low Friday, then closed back above it. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Hirsch likes the timing. "Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," he said. His firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday. Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596. Losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play. That's about 21% below Friday's close. The case for waiting Not everyone is loading up the shopping cart. BofA's Michael Hartnett said it's "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday , but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which closed Friday near $522. On SOXX, that works out to about $469, just above the July low it barely held. So the bulls' and bears' lines sit almost on top of each other. Hirsch said he'd change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close. Tuesday's midterm vote comes first. Then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year , gets its turn. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: Trump calls $50 million contract for ex-lawyer Habba Mildon 'not acceptable'
articles.summary: By Gram Slattery and Jasper Ward PALM BEACH, Oct 31 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Saturday it was "unacceptable" for one of his ‌former lawyers, Alina Habba Mildon, to secure a $50 million contract for ‌herself while working at the US Department of Justice. "I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, ​and it's not acceptable," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. "Not acceptable at all." The New York Times reported last week that the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a Venezuelan banker facing US felony bribery charges before ‌striking a plea deal in ⁠August 2025, guaranteed Habba Mildon more than $50 million over four years. The deal, according to the newspaper, would pay $10 million a ⁠year plus bonuses. Trump said he told Habba Mildon he did not want her to be paid and called the episode "terrible." Habba Mildon was serving as the acting US attorney ​in New ​Jersey when she signed the contract with ​Herrera's family company, Concord Partners, ‌days after it was registered in late October 2025, the New York Times reported. By the time she started her employment with the Herrera family, a court had disqualified her from serving as US attorney. She resigned on December 8 and was appointed a senior adviser to the attorney general the same day, ‌and was still in that role when, ​according to the New York Times, she started ​at Concord on January 1. Trump ​pardoned Herrera on January 15, 2026, according to the Justice ‌Department's website. Habba Mildon last week said ​she was never paid ​for a pardon, never met with anyone at the White House or Justice Department about a pardon, and never did any work for ​a pardon for anyone. The ‌Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. (Reporting by ​Gram Slattery in Palm Beach and Jasper Ward in Washington; ​Editing by Sergio Non and Lincoln Feast.) articles.title: Trump admin lays groundwork to challenge midterm results after Election Day
articles.summary: In the closing days of a campaign for Congress where polls show his side losing, President Donald Trump and his Justice Department are filing lawsuits and opening investigations that could extend disputes well beyond Election Day. The administration's extraordinary attempt to cast doubt on the midterm elections, discount some ballots and prevent the finalization of results is entering a frenetic new phase. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The litigation strategy has failed so far, but appears designed to give the Justice Department more time to contest results after the election. Trump, worried about a Democratic takeover of Congress and a third impeachment, has tilted the Justice Department away from its traditional role of easing access to the ballot and toward erecting last-minute hurdles that could prevent some people from voting. It is trying to force California to set aside thousands of ballots and Alaska to hold off on certifying the results if a Democrat wins the state's Senate race. It has threatened to sue Washington state if it doesn't discount ballots from hundreds of voters and suggested it may try to do the same in other states. Administration officials have struggled in court so far, in part because the Constitution puts states - not the federal government - in charge of running elections. "A lot of what you're seeing is just a sort of a temper tantrum in the form of a lawsuit," said Sam Oliker-Friedland, a former frontline voting rights litigator at the Justice Department who now leads the Institute for Responsive Government. One of the Justice Department's most aggressive moves is in California, where it has sued to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 voters who it says may be noncitizens. It has also warned election officials it could charge them with aiding and abetting illegal voting if they count the ballots of noncitizens. Last week, a federal grand jury issued subpoenas to Los Angeles County officials for emails, text messages and other communications about how it handled the Justice Department's demands. It's not clear whether the targets of the investigation are election officials, voters or someone else. District U.S. Judge David O. Carter this week ruled against the department, saying its plan to set aside ballots would probably violate the Voting Rights Act, the Civil Rights Act and the National Voter Registration Act. "It would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately," Carter warned Justice Department lawyers at the end of a lengthy hearing on the eve of his decision. His decision was upheld Friday by a panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on a two-one vote. The majority said the Justice Department had not identified any federal authority giving it the ability to "take charge of or intervene in a state's administration of an ongoing election." It was the third adverse ruling for the Justice Department in the case this week, including one in which a judge wrote that the administration's plans could lead to electoral chaos. Also on Friday, a federal judge in San Francisco issued a sweeping emergency order barring the department from making any further demands that election workers in California remove voters from the rolls or not count specific ballots. The ruling, which came in response to a suit from unions that represent election officials in California, also prohibited Justice Department officials from threatening to prosecute election administrators who do not accede to their orders. "When state and local government employees perform the work of distributing, processing, or counting ballots or otherwise administering the 2026 midterm election in the manner required by their state and federal laws governing the administration of elections," wrote U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson, a Biden appointee, "they do not violate federal criminal law even if a particular ballot belongs to a registered voter alleged by [the administration] to be ineligible to vote." Breaking the firewall A transformation of the Justice Department began soon after Trump was sworn in last year. Top officials turned their attention to investigating the president's political enemies, and in recent weeks have escalated such probes despite a decades-long tradition of holding off on politically charged cases in the 60 days before an election. Longtime attorneys with the Civil Rights Division - a bulwark protecting voting rights for decades - quit or were fired and were replaced with political appointees. The Justice Department last year demanded that states turn over voter rolls that include sensitive data such as partial Social Security numbers. Most didn't, and the Justice Department sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for them. It has lost all 27 of the cases that have been decided so far. Lacking the full voter rolls for California and other states, the administration has been using incomplete versions to try to find noncitizens, who are banned from voting in federal elections. The approach is flawed and some citizens are wrongly getting tagged as noncitizens, election officials say. They are fighting the administration's efforts because they say they fear qualified voters' ballots could be discounted. Since the start of Trump's second term, the department has charged almost 200 people in 22 states with illegally voting or registering to vote as noncitizens, a fraction of the tens of millions of people who typically vote in major elections. More than 70 percent of those cases were filed in the past two months, including 18 more announced Thursday in North Carolina. On Thursday, in another signal that disputes could stretch beyond when races get called, the Justice Department sent letters to election administrators in every state reminding them to preserve poll books and other election records and threatening prosecution if they don't. The letters were signed by acting deputy attorney general Trent McCotter, the department's No. 2 official. "Cracking down on illegal voting [and] investigating these cases is not a threat to elections," McCotter told reporters. "It's not a threat to democracy; it's not a threat to election officials. Exactly the opposite. We're trying to ensure that every citizen has their vote counted, and that it's not canceled out by someone who's not allowed to." DOJ targets Alaska race In Alaska, the Justice Department is taking a different, but no less unusual, approach. This month it sued the state to prevent it from certifying the results if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the race for Senate. It argues voters may be confused because one candidate in the race, Dan J. Sullivan, shares a nearly identical name with the incumbent, Republican Dan S. Sullivan. On Friday, it asked a judge to order the state to segregate some ballots. Robert Weiner, who served as senior counsel in the Civil Rights Division during President Joe Biden's administration, said he considers the cases in Alaska and California flimsy and a "desperate" attempt to challenge results the administration does not like. The approach departs from the Justice Department's long-standing independence from the White House, he said. "It appears that the Justice Department follows Attorney General [Todd] Blanche's view that he works for Trump," said Weiner, director of voting rights for the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. Election law experts say the administration's attempt to potentially block certification of Alaska's vote is based on an unprecedented interpretation of federal law. The suit relies on a novel reading of the National Voter Registration Act, a statute that governs voter registration requirements, not candidate eligibility or election administration. Justice Department lawyers have cited a snippet of the introduction to that law that says it was passed to "protect the integrity of the electoral process" to justify its attempt to intervene in that race. If backed by the courts in the Alaska suit, that interpretation could lay the groundwork for a wave of litigation in states where the department takes issue with how the election plays out. Using the law that way would amount to "a limitless grant of authority for federal interference in state-run elections," attorneys representing Alaska wrote in a filing Thursday, urging a judge to reject that interpretation. The suit calls for Alaska's results to be put on hold if Sen. Sullivan narrowly loses so an investigation can determine whether voters intended that result. But the department has not indicated how it foresees carrying out such an investigation while protecting ballot secrecy. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which could further complicate any review of the results. As the lawsuit proceeds through the courts, the Justice Department is conducting a separate criminal investigation into the origins of Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. That inquiry gained new life this week when the New York Times reported Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting him to run, which Peltola denies. Federal prosecutors issued dozens of subpoenas and record preservation notices this week seeking access to text messages and other communications referenced in the Times report, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. While the potential targets of that investigation remain uncertain, a department official said prosecutors are exploring the possibility of civil rights charges alleging a conspiracy to deprive Alaska voters of their right to a fair election. "Every Alaskan deserves a fair election," Alaska's U.S. attorney, Michael J. Heyman, told reporters Friday. "And they're going to get one." Annie Gowen and Perry Stein contributed to this report. articles.title: 70GW“电力缺口”！美国电网、民众和AI巨头，总得有一方“让步”，天量资本开支“无法落地”
articles.summary: 人工智能的爆发式增长正与美国电网的物理极限发生激烈碰撞，由此产生的巨大电力缺口，正对全球科技巨头的基础设施扩张计划构成实质性威胁。需求与供给之间的严重错配意味着， 市场预期的天量AI资本开支正面临“无法落地”的严峻风险 ，而电网、民众与科技巨头之间的博弈已进入白热化阶段。 据摩根士丹利分析师Stephen Byrd的最新测算， 美国数据中心开发商在2028年前面临高达70GW的电力缺口 。即使穷尽所有潜在的解决方案，包括核能、燃料电池以及将部分需求转移至亚洲， 净电力缺口依然高达43GW 。这一数字在短短一年内激增了超过两倍，凸显了物理基础设施对AI产业发展的硬性制约。 这一供需失衡正在迅速重塑市场定价与资本流向。 一方面，能够提供“电力交付时效”（time to power）解决方案的设备供应商正获得极高的溢价，燃气轮机等核心设备价格已飙升两倍；另一方面，随着电力成本上升和地方反对声浪加剧，信贷市场对AI相关债务的态度正变得挑剔。投资者愈发担忧，部分庞大的数据中心建设计划最终将被迫延期或取消。 在电力成本飙升的背景下，美国民众对新建数据中心的反对情绪日益高涨， 多州政府已开始实施项目审批冻结 。市场正面临一个冷酷的现实：要么科技巨头被迫削减其宏大的产能规划，要么在获取电力的过程中承担前所未有的延期与成本代价。 尽管美国能源信息署（EIA）的最新数据显示，美国电网在9月份实现了十年来最强劲的产能增长，但这掩盖了深层次的结构性危机。新增产能的类型、地理位置和并网时间，完全无法匹配数据中心全天候运转的严苛需求。整个行业正陷入由设备短缺、劳动力断层和政策阻力交织而成的多重瓶颈之中。 70GW缺口：最重要的约束仍是电力 摩根士丹利的AlphaWise调查清晰揭示了这场危机的核心症结所在。 调查显示，"电力接入速度"是全球数据中心运营商反映的首要瓶颈，占比27%；在美国，这一比例高达45%，远超其他任何国家。"已供电土地的可用性"排名第二，美国同样以26%居全球首位。 摩根士丹利的测算框架如下： 美国数据中心开发商到2028年合计需要116GW电力。在建数据中心（含独立供电项目）覆盖25GW，可用电网接入覆盖21GW，由此产生70GW毛缺口。加计"快速供电"解决方案——合适的核电站选址（2GW）、已公告的涡轮机和发动机（20GW）、Bloom燃料电池（5GW）、美国需求向亚洲溢出（5GW）——净缺口仍达38GW，约为所需电力总量的33%。 摩根士丹利的美国数据中心团队以电力公司口径重新表述：2028年需求180GW对阵供给137GW，43GW的缺口较当前的15GW近乎扩大三倍。 需求激增与“无效”供给：电网结构的错配 华尔街投行正以前所未有的幅度上调电力需求预期。 Bernstein分析师Sunaina Ocalan将其 对2030年前美国电力需求的复合年增长率（CAGR）预测从3%上调至4% 。 该机构预计，2025年至2030年间， 美国将新增约1000太瓦时（TWh）的电力需求，其中超过一半由数据中心贡献 。 高盛的模型同样显示，到2030年，美国数据中心的电力需求将从2025年的39GW攀升至108GW。 然而， 供给端的结构性错配令这一需求增长显得岌岌可危。 高盛的数据显示，9月份美国电网净增5.6GW发电能力，但主要由太阳能（3.0GW）和电池储能（1.6GW）构成。对于需要24小时不间断运行的数据中心而言，太阳能的容量系数仅约为25%，无法提供稳定的基载电力。 能够满足这一需求的天然气发电产能建设则严重滞后。 9月份，作为基载主力的联合循环燃气电厂新增产能为零。高盛指出， 天然气发电项目的集中交付期要到2028年至2030年才会到来，这恰好错过了摩根士丹利预测的电力缺口高峰期 。这种时间上的错位意味着，在未来几年内，电网根本无法提供足够且合适的电力来支撑AI的扩张。 供应链与劳动力的双重枷锁 即使资金充裕，物理世界的供应链和劳动力短缺也构成了难以逾越的障碍。 在设备端，摩根士丹利指出，GE Vernova的燃气轮机订单已排至2029年， 其价格已从2020年代初的每千瓦1000美元飙升至3000美元 。大型电力变压器的交货期长达3至4年，开关设备也需要1至2年。设备成本的全面上涨导致数据中心的建设成本大幅攀升，预计到本年代末，每GW的建设成本将从2022/23年的300亿美元增至500亿至600亿美元。 比设备更棘手的是人力资源。 高盛估计，到2030年，美国电力行业将需要超过50万名新工人。即使在最乐观的学徒培训假设下， 输配电领域到2030年仍将面临78000人的劳动力缺口。 Bernstein分析师Chad Dillard基于现有电工、管道工和暖通空调技术人员的物理建设能力建立的模型显示， 劳动力短缺可能成为最坚硬的制约因素 ，将2030年的IT容量部署上限锁定在142GW，远低于市场的乐观预期。 巨头的自救与“电表后”发电的兴起 面对电网的迟缓，科技巨头正在采取绕过传统电网的自救措施。高盛预计，到2030年，独立供电（Behind-the-Meter，BTM，即不经过公共电网直接为用户供电）将为25%的数据中心提供动力。摩根士丹利则更为激进，预测到2030年美国BTM需求将达到47GW。 摩根士丹利基准情景假设2028年前将新增约20GW的BTM燃气涡轮机和发动机（区间6至38GW），叠加约6GW在建装机及6GW Bloom燃料电池。其美国数据中心团队追踪到2026至2028年制造商订单达25至30GW，并预计开发商从2028年起每年可新增15GW以上BTM产能。但即便是最乐观的"快速供电"组合方案，仍将留下17GW的净缺口（基准情景下为38GW）。 核能成为了另一个备受追捧的选项。 谷歌、亚马逊等巨头近期频繁与Constellation等核电运营商达成协议，试图通过重启现有反应堆或提升现有产能来获取电力。然而，远水难解近渴。摩根士丹利指出，新建大型核电站的交货期长达约15年，而小型模块化反应堆（SMR）的商业化部署要到2030年代中期才能实现，完全无法填补2028年的缺口。 在这一过程中， 科技巨头对电价几乎不敏感 。摩根士丹利的分析显示，即使电价上涨17%（从120美元/兆瓦时升至140美元/兆瓦时），一个100MW的AI数据中心的股本回报率（ROE）仅会下降约60个基点，依然能 保持在30%以上 。这种对价格的不敏感，正将压力转嫁给普通纳税人和电网系统。 民众反弹与政策阻力：谁来买单？ 科技巨头愿意支付高昂的电价，但普通民众和选民却不愿为此买单。摩根士丹利估计，今年全球电价上涨了约20%。在PJM（美国最大的区域电网运营商）的最近四次容量拍卖中，数据中心占据了46%的成本。 电费的飙升引发了强烈的政治反弹。盖洛普的最新民调显示， 70%的美国人反对在当地社区建设数据中心 ，且这种反对跨越了党派界限。各州政府已开始采取行动：德克萨斯州在9月份下令暂停新建数据中心，并对ERCOT（德州电网）互连流程中的所有项目展开审计；宾夕法尼亚州取消了快速审批通道；纽约州则暂停了50MW以上数据中心的环境许可。 政策阻力直接导致了资本开支的停滞。摩根士丹利的数据显示，2023年有约1560亿美元的数据中心项目被取消或延期，2024年第一季度这一数字达到1300亿美元。随着AI相关债务发行量在今年达到4710亿美元，信贷市场正变得愈发谨慎。 如果物理电力无法到位， 天量资本开支计划面临被迫搁置的风险 。在2030年数据中心预计将消耗美国七分之一电力的背景下，电网、民众与AI巨头之间，注定将有一方必须做出妥协。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 公开“叛党”、低级搅局！美国中选最后时刻“精彩纷呈”
articles.summary: 美国中期选举于11月3日举行，共和党与民主党围绕国会两院及州级、地方席位展开激烈争夺。然而，选举前的最后阶段，美国多州接连曝出多起“闹剧”。 民主党方面，一起是公开的“党内叛变”，另一起是精心策划的选票搅局阴谋。 密歇根州，民主党众议员Haley Stevens在选前最后一个周日公开转身，为共和党参议员候选人Mike Rogers站台背书。阿拉斯加州，据当地媒体的深度调查则揭露，民主党参议员候选人Mary Peltola的竞选团队耗费数月，秘密招募与共和党现任参议员同名的"幌子候选人"参选，试图以混淆选民姓名的方式分流对手选票。 共和党方面，则出现“母女反目”、“广告互攻”等戏剧性局面。 据 新华社 ，在俄亥俄州州长选举中，共和党候选人维韦克·拉马斯瓦米利用民主党对手埃米·阿克顿的生母拍摄攻击性竞选广告引发巨大争议。 共和党与民主党在冲刺阶段的内部管控与选举策略，正面临严峻考验。无论周二选举结果如何，这些裂痕都不会随之消失。 密歇根：公开叛党，党内哗然 据媒体11月1日报道，Haley Stevens在周日发布于X平台的视频中宣布支持共和党候选人Rogers称："我不属于Abdul的竞选阵营。"她还表示，自己也不认同El-Sayed竞选团队中左翼网络主播Hasan Piker等人的立场，"我热爱这个州……我在这里宣示我们密歇根人的身份。" Stevens此前在8月初选中以不足一个百分点的差距败给民主党参议员候选人Abdul El-Sayed，随后勉强背书对方。但两人关系始终冰冷。 矛盾在近日激化。Stevens要求El-Sayed就其对以色列的批评公开道歉，并要求他与一则她认为带有反犹色彩的外部广告划清界限。El-Sayed则表示不认同该广告内容，并指责Stevens转移竞选核心议题。 周日，Stevens现身底特律一座教堂，与Rogers同台亮相。她对记者说："我站在党这边，却被人从台上嘘下去。" El-Sayed随后在另一座教堂外回应记者时只说了一句话："这些都无关紧要。" Stevens的“叛党”举动在民主党内引发强烈谴责。参议院少数党领袖Chuck Schumer发表声明，称此举是"来自Haley Stevens众议员的卑鄙背叛"。 即将卸任的密歇根州参议员Gary Peters则表示对Stevens的决定"极度失望"。 Stevens自己的国会办公室也随之陷入混乱。她的幕僚长Justin German发表声明，称自己和多名工作人员对这一背书决定"震惊且心碎"，并宣布辞职。"这场选举太重要了，不能制造分裂或袖手旁观，"German写道，并呼吁选民投票支持El-Sayed。媒体记者向Stevens的新闻主任Logan Basch发送置评请求，收到的自动回复显示："您好，自11月1日起，我已不再在Haley Stevens众议员办公室任职。" 阿拉斯加：同名搅局，两个“Dan Sullivan” 阿拉斯加的故事更为复杂。据媒体深度调查，早在2025年夏，Mary Peltola的竞选团队工作人员就收到了一项不寻常的指令：在阿拉斯加找出所有名叫Dan Sullivan的人。 原因显而易见。 Dan S. Sullivan是该州现任共和党参议员的名字。如果能说服另一个同名者参选，就可能在该州特殊的四人选票制度下制造混淆，分流现任参议员的选票。 计划奏效了。今年春天，一名来自阿拉斯加狭长地带偏远渔村、只能靠空运和海运抵达的退休教师宣布参选参议员，他的名字是Dan J. Sullivan。 报道基于对12名知情人士的采访、数十条短信记录，以及为潜在诉讼准备的文件。报道的核心信源是Peltola的前竞选经理Elisa Rios——她在8月的团队重组中被解雇，此后接受了该报的系列采访。 "阿拉斯加选民需要知道真相，"Rios说，"有很多猜测，选民在做决定时应该得到完整的信息。" 她表示，Peltola本人并未直接参与该项目，但"肯定知情"。 据报道，这场同名行动在内部被称为"选票构成项目"，核心人物是一名来自俄亥俄州的民主党资深操盘手Jerid Kurtz。他由民主党参议员竞选委员会（DSCC）的工作人员引荐给Peltola团队，被介绍为"秘密选票操作专家"。Kurtz在行动中使用化名和掩护故事，以"Zane"的身份在阿拉斯加各地活动，在酒吧里向潜在候选人游说。 Rios描述了Kurtz汇报找到Dan J. Sullivan时的情形。Kurtz说，这位Sullivan"说他讨厌特朗普，如果这能帮助Mary，他喜欢Mary。他对当政客没有兴趣，但如果这能有所帮助……" Peltola竞选团队否认招募“幌子候选人” Peltola竞选团队和DSCC均否认参与招募幌子候选人。"阿拉斯加人支持Mary Peltola竞选团队与任何Sullivan竞选团队均无关联，也未招募任何候选人参选，"该团队在声明中表示。DSCC发表类似声明，称对招募Sullivan或"任何其他共和党候选人""毫不知情"。 司法部已应特朗普要求向联邦法院提起诉讼，寻求在Dan J. Sullivan的选票导致现任参议员落败时阻止认证选举结果。 但法律专家对此持怀疑态度。前共和党全国委员会总法律顾问Benjamin Ginsberg对彭博表示："这完全是以法律行动为幌子的政治表演。"加州大学洛杉矶分校选举法学者Rick Hasen同样认为，司法部试图以"剥夺选民宪法权利"为由起诉相关人员的理论"很可能遭遇第一修正案障碍"。 在政治层面，彭博观点专栏作家Ronald Brownstein指出，该丑闻的最大杀伤力在于，它与Peltola的核心竞选叙事直接矛盾——她一直将自己塑造为关注普通阿拉斯加人的"局外人"，将现任参议员Sullivan（俄亥俄州移民）描绘为"华盛顿腐败体制的化身"。"现在看起来，是她这边在试图操弄规则，"Brownstein写道。 不过，阿拉斯加领先的独立民调人士Ivan Moore对彭博表示，该争议"最可能的结果是几乎没有任何影响"。 俄亥俄州：母女反目 除密歇根州和阿拉斯加州外，多地竞选在最后阶段仍围绕个人经历、广告创意和履历争议展开。 据新华社报道，在俄亥俄州州长选举中，共和党候选人维韦克·拉马斯瓦米利用民主党对手埃米·阿克顿的生母拍摄攻击性竞选广告引发巨大争议。 拉马斯瓦米的竞选团队邀请阿克顿的母亲唐娜·阿瑟出镜制作广告并耗巨资推广。唐娜·阿瑟在广告中称女儿是“骗子”“有严重问题”，否认女儿童年受虐和无家可归等经历，并呼吁选民不要让女儿选上州长。 该广告在社交媒体发布后引发批评，俄亥俄州共和党籍州长Mike DeWine也对广告提出批评；特朗普和副总统万斯则公开支持播放该广告。 得州：广告互攻 在得州参议员选举中，共和党候选人、得州总检察长Ken Paxton与民主党候选人James Talarico的广告战持续升温。新华社报道称，双方竞选团队累计投入已超过5亿美元，可能成为美国历史上最昂贵的参议员选举之一。 Paxton团队的一则广告中，一只手从电线杆上取下失踪儿童的寻人启事，意在突出其打击人口贩卖的政绩。但广告因“撕掉寻人启事”的画面受到民主党人和网民嘲讽。 Talarico团队则推出一款虚构的体育博彩应用广告，让观众预测Paxton的“下一桩丑闻”。广告称：“这个应用程序是假的，但Ken Paxton的丑闻是真的。” 对市场和政策观察者而言，焦点并不止于单一席位胜负。若阿拉斯加州计票、排名选择投票和诉讼程序同步拉长，参议院控制权的最终确认时间可能被推迟，选后政治不确定性也将随之延续。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 与前两次打击前夕类似！特朗普“打谈并举”，海湾国家“忧虑重重”
articles.summary: 中期选举后美国对伊朗发动新一轮打击的可能性正在上升，局势走向牵动全球市场神经。特朗普政府延续其在"午夜之锤行动"和"史诗怒火行动"前夕的一贯模式——一边推进外交谈判，一边为军事行动保留选项。与此同时，海湾国家对可能到来的新一轮冲突深感忧虑，担心伊朗的报复将比此前更为猛烈。 据央视新闻，据以色列方面11月1日消息，以色列和美国消息人士透露，美国总统特朗普与以色列总理内塔尼亚胡10月31日就美国与伊朗的谈判进行了一次“直接而尖锐”的通话。消息人士称，内塔尼亚胡敦促特朗普在11月3日美国中期选举结束后“立即恢复对伊朗的战争”，并对目前在卡塔尔斡旋下进行的美伊谈判感到担忧。 特朗普现阶段则希望“让谈判充分展开”，不希望以色列干扰谈判进程。据悉，如果谈判失败，特朗普的立场可能发生“显著变化”。 海湾国家对局势的走向忧心忡忡。 据媒体报道，伊朗最高领袖哈梅内伊周六已命令军方做好"无地理限制"的即时反击准备，并扩大潜在打击目标清单。国际货币基金组织预测沙特经济今年将萎缩3.3%，科威特和卡塔尔的收缩幅度预计更为严峻。 对投资者而言，一旦新一轮冲突爆发，油价上行压力、地区供应链中断以及资产避险情绪将是最直接的市场冲击。 "打谈并举"：特朗普再度走双轨路线 据媒体报道，特朗普正在重复其在2025年6月"午夜之锤行动"和2026年2月"史诗怒火行动"前夕的操作模式——同步推进外交接触与军事准备。 上周，副总统万斯致函伊朗国家安全负责人Mohsen Rezaei，提议重启直接谈判，并强调伊朗核计划必须作为谈判起点。这是美国数月来级别最高的对伊外交接触。与此同时，卡塔尔调停人连续三天与伊朗官员会面，斡旋重启直接谈判的可能性。 然而，特朗普的表态颇为矛盾。 他一方面告诉记者谈判"进展顺利"，自己"不太着急"；另一方面又明确指出伊朗"不太可靠，达成协议后又反悔"，并公开点名Pickaxe Mountain这一疑似核设施，称美国"已有计划，可以很快处理"。 伊朗外长Abbas Araghchi周日表示，目前尚未达成任何协议，能否取得进展取决于美方对伊朗问题的回应。调停方正在讨论一项方案，若美方满足伊朗条件，霍尔木兹海峡可在两天内重新开放，但谈判分歧依然巨大——伊朗要求美方先解除海上封锁、放宽制裁并解冻资产，华盛顿则坚持要求伊朗先作出核领域让步。 特朗普寻找"替罪羊"，五角大楼内部暗流涌动 随着中期选举前景黯淡，特朗普正在追究这场战争的责任归属，并将矛头指向曾向他保证战争将"速战速决"的顾问们。 两名特朗普圈外顾问透露， 特朗普近期一直在向盟友打探国防部长Pete Hegseth和参谋长联席会议主席Dan Caine的工作表现。Hegseth和Caine是这场战争的主要推手，也是早期最为乐观的公开倡导者——但两人自5月以来再未召开过新闻发布会。 特朗普的不满有迹可循。媒体援引知情人士，Hegseth惯于向总统报喜不报忧，"擅长告诉总统他想听的话"。五角大楼发言人Sean Parnell对此予以否认，称Hegseth"始终向总统提供完整的作战全貌"。 与此同时，Hegseth上周突然解雇了参谋长联席会议最高级别军官之一、陆军中将Brett Sylvia，理由是其在泄露信息调查中未能通过测谎测试。此举在五角大楼内部引发强烈震动。部分官员认为，Hegseth此举意在削弱参谋长联席会议的地位，以便在总统评估战争成效之际为自己争取更有利的位置。 媒体援引一名官员的说法称，Hegseth此前曾在戴维营向特朗普暗示，弹药短缺问题应由副部长Stephen Feinberg负责——尽管Feinberg至今仍在职。 军事选项"无一令人满意"，打击效果存疑 据媒体报道，摆在特朗普面前的军事选项涵盖数小时、数天乃至数周不等的打击方案，也包括维持霍尔木兹海峡封锁同时保留军事威慑，或直接撤出。中央司令部司令Brad Cooper上周也出席了白宫的方案汇报会议。 然而，熟悉相关计划的现任及前任国防官员坦言，这些选项"无一令人满意"。智库史汀生中心研究美国军事干预成本效益的Michael Cohen表示："如果打击不奏效，你就暴露了这些打击的局限性。你不断打击，他们不退让，那你还能怎么办？不断升级吗？" 数月的空袭未能摧毁伊朗的导弹和无人机制造能力。 西方官员10月曾表示，伊朗已保留足够的生产能力来补充武器库存，目前仍储有大量弹道导弹和部分反舰武器， 俄罗斯也在持续供应 导弹。截至10月初，伊朗自2月28日战争爆发以来已发射逾4000枚沙赫德无人机和至少2000枚弹道导弹。 国际战略研究所地区安全主任Emile Hokayem指出，伊朗在2月28日遭受打击后展现出更强的军事学习和适应能力，"这表明伊朗能够与对手抗衡"。 海湾国家：承受代价，却无力左右局势 据媒体报道，在巴林马纳麦举行的国际战略研究所对话论坛上，海湾国家官员罕见地集体表达了对新一轮冲突的深切忧虑。 阿联酋总统外交顾问Anwar Gargash表示，"我们发现自己被卷入一场我们曾竭力通过外交手段加以避免的危机"，并强调各方正在寻求"政治出路"。海合会秘书长Jasem Al-Budaiwi则明确指出，"海合会国家不是这场战争的当事方，也从未寻求这场战争"。 皇家联合服务研究所国际安全副研究员Mohammed al-Basha表示，"我没有听到任何一位海湾官员或平民支持美以对伊朗发动新的打击，但大多数人感到新一轮打击迫在眉睫"，并警告伊朗这一轮将"更具攻击性，不会遵守此前观察到的交战规则"。 埃及外长Badr Abdelatty在论坛上直言"极度担忧"，称"第二轮将更危险、更具破坏性，且不会带来任何结果"。 伊朗的最新表态进一步加剧了这种担忧。最高领袖哈梅内伊周六命令军方做好"无地理限制"的即时反击准备，并扩大潜在打击目标清单。伊朗军方警告，一旦美以再度发动攻击，战火将蔓延至更大范围。 国际战略研究所高级研究员Hasan Alhasan的评价颇为严峻："如果说1991年美国解放科威特是确立美国在该地区角色的时刻，那么2026年这场战争或许将被铭记为瓦解这一角色的时刻。" 风险提示及免责条款
